clue.text: Provided by the press to those sleeping rough?

definitions.text: Provided by the press to those sleeping rough?

parts.words: Provided by the press to those sleeping rough?
parts.note: newspapers handed out at no charge, read as bed linen given away to homeless people

explanation.surface: A charitable press hands out something to people sleeping on the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'press' is the newspaper industry, but a rough sleeper would welcome bedding given away for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers distributed at no cost to readers, paid for by advertising, are called by this name.

clue.text: Hornblower sailed with one such (a cutter)

definitions.text: Hornblower sailed with one such (a cutter)

parts.words: Hornblower sailed with one such (a cutter)
parts.note: C. S. Forester's novel Hornblower and the Atropos names his ship after the mythical sister who cuts the thread of life

explanation.surface: A naval captain's voyage on a small sailing vessel called a cutter.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is a kind of ship, which suits Hornblower; here it is Atropos, the one of the three Greek goddesses of destiny who cuts each life's thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropos is one of the three Moirai, the Greek goddesses of destiny, and she severs the thread of each life.

clue.text: London garden?

parts.note: Jack London wrote the novel Martin ___, whose surname is also the biblical paradise garden

explanation.surface: A green space in the British capital.
explanation.walkthrough: London is the American novelist Jack London, not the city: his hero is Martin Eden, and the surname is also the garden of Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical paradise where Adam lived is a garden, and Jack London's novel takes that word as its hero's surname.

clue.text: Amis's pet ague deteriorates due to tape misusage three weeks before Lent

indicators.note: something that deteriorates falls apart, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: the name Amis with its possessive s kept as a letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A novelist's fever worsens because he misuses sticky tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deteriorates' shuffles AMISSPETAGUE; 'due to tape misusage' offers a second anagram of the same twelve letters, TAPE MISUSAGE, with 'misusage' as its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth Sunday before Easter, about two and a half weeks ahead of Ash Wednesday, is named from the Latin for seventieth.

clue.text: He knew he was right

parts.note: Trollope's novel He Knew He Was Right has as its jealous husband Louis, whose surname is wanted

explanation.surface: A stubborn man was certain of his own correctness.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is the title of a Trollope novel, and 'He' is its central character, the obsessively jealous Louis.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis, the husband driven mad by suspicion in Trollope's novel, bears this surname.

clue.text: Interior seascape, perhaps, by Masefield hero

definitions.text: Interior seascape, perhaps, by Masefield hero

parts.words: Interior seascape, perhaps, by Masefield hero
parts.note: a poor painting of the sea such as the amateur artist in Masefield's poem ... might produce

explanation.surface: A painting of the sea made by a character from a John Masefield poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Masefield's narrative poem Dauber follows a sailor who tries to paint the sea; his nickname comes from the crude work he turns out.
explanation.definitionFit: A crude, clumsily painted picture is called this, and the Dauber's nickname comes from such work.

clue.text: Thomas Nashe said that it fell from the air during the plague

definitions.text: Thomas Nashe said that it fell from the air during the plague

parts.words: Thomas Nashe said that it fell from the air during the plague
parts.note: the line from Nashe's song in Summer's Last Will and Testament, written in a time of pestilence: '___ falls from the air'

explanation.surface: An Elizabethan writer reports something dropping from the sky during an epidemic.
explanation.walkthrough: Nashe's 'Litany in Time of Plague' says 'Brightness falls from the air; / Queens have died young and fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of shining or radiance, which Nashe pictures falling from the sky in his plague litany.

clue.text: An intruder in the Lawrence canon

definitions.meaning: someone who enters land without permission
D. H. Lawrence's second novel bears this title

explanation.surface: Someone unwelcome has crept into the works of D. H. Lawrence.
explanation.definitionFit: An intruder on private land, and the title of Lawrence's 1912 novel about an ill-fated affair.

clue.text: Case for beginning Elizabeth Taylor's underrated imaginings

indicators.note: the beginning of each of the following four words is taken

explanation.surface: An argument for appreciating the novelist Elizabeth Taylor's undervalued fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like an argument being made, but it is the definition; the novelist Elizabeth Taylor is a nice literary touch.
explanation.definitionFit: A small ornamental container for needles and sewing items is called by this name.

clue.text: Two score Frenchmen who live for ever

definitions.text: Two score Frenchmen who live for ever

parts.words: Two score Frenchmen who live for ever
parts.note: the forty members of the Académie française, nicknamed the immortals

explanation.surface: Forty Frenchmen are mysteriously immortal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Académie française has forty seats, and its members are called 'les immortels'.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of an academy, here the forty-strong French learned body whose members are called immortal.

clue.text: It's said a queue formed to identify his work

definitions.text: It's said a queue formed to identify his work

parts.words: It's said a queue formed to identify his work
parts.note: the Cornish author signed his writing with the single letter Q, which sounds like the word queue

explanation.surface: Readers lined up to recognise a writer's books.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter Q sounds like 'queue'; Sir Arthur, editor of the Oxford Book of English Verse, published under that one-letter pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur, the Cornish novelist and anthologist, signed his work with the single initial Q.

clue.text: Dido's feted barbarically on bardic occasion

indicators.note: treating the words barbarically mangles their letters into a new order

parts.note: the name Dido with its possessive s kept as a letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: The queen of Carthage is celebrated with savage festivities at a poetry gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barbarically' rearranges DIDOSFETED.
explanation.definitionFit: A Welsh festival of poetry and music where bards compete for prizes.

clue.text: Literary crime of which Sheridan's fretful character was guilty

definitions.text: Literary crime of which Sheridan's fretful character was guilty

parts.words: Literary crime of which Sheridan's fretful character was guilty
parts.note: Sir Fretful Plagiary in Sheridan's comedy The Critic is named for stealing other writers' work

explanation.surface: A Sheridan character committed a crime in the world of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's The Critic, Sir Fretful Plagiary is a touchy playwright whose name says he passes off others' work as his own.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing off another writer's words as one's own, the offence Sir Fretful's surname announces.

clue.text: How a mystery author writes to deepen the enigma?

definitions.text: How a mystery author writes to deepen the enigma?

parts.words: How a mystery author writes to deepen the enigma?
parts.note: a writer of detective fiction whose handwriting cannot be read makes the puzzle even harder

explanation.surface: A crime novelist's technique for making the plot more puzzling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writes' seems to mean composing a plot, but it is literal handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing so badly formed that it cannot be read would certainly add to a mystery.

clue.text: Poet's version offered by Rattigan

parts.note: Terence Rattigan's play is called The ___ Version, named after Robert the Victorian poet

explanation.surface: A dramatist presents his own take on a poet's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Rattigan's play The Browning Version is about a schoolmaster given Browning's translation of the Agamemnon.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert, the Victorian poet, made the translation of Aeschylus that gives Rattigan's play its title.

clue.text: Listener expects to find this spirit in a bottle

definitions.text: Listener expects to find this spirit in a bottle

parts.words: Listener expects to find this spirit in a bottle
parts.note: a genie traditionally lives in a bottle, and to someone hearing the word it sounds like the drink gin, also found in a bottle

explanation.surface: Someone expects a supernatural being to be trapped in a flask.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is said like 'gin', a spirit that comes in bottles, while the genie of stories also lives in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A supernatural being of Arabian folklore, the genie, often pictured confined in a lamp or flask.

clue.text: To speak at random and describe Roman attire

parts.note: to gas is to chatter idly

explanation.surface: Talking freely about the clothing of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose outer garments worn by citizens of ancient Rome.

clue.text: "And hide with — their want of art" (Pope)

definitions.text: "And hide with — their want of art" (Pope)

parts.words: "And hide with — their want of art" (Pope)
parts.note: the closing line of a couplet in Pope's Essay on Criticism about poets covering every part with gold and jewels

explanation.surface: A line from Alexander Pope with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's Essay on Criticism: 'With gold and jewels cover every part, / And hide with ornaments their want of art.'
explanation.definitionFit: Decorations such as gold and jewels, which Pope says poor poets heap on to conceal a lack of skill.

clue.text: 12's music for one gone before (4)

definitions.note: a work by the author at 12 across

indicators.note: the dead person's phrase comes before the word for music

parts.note: one who has gone is a dead man; with the possessive for 'for'
rock is a style of popular music

explanation.surface: A piece of music played in memory of someone who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is Quiller-Couch, whose first novel, an adventure story, has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiller-Couch's first novel, an 1887 adventure story, carries this title.

clue.text: Poet comes up in talk of gardenia, rose and fuchsia

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the poet is found inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A poet crops up in conversation about flowers in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds ENIAR across 'gardenia, rose'; 'comes up' turns it round for Kathleen Raine.
explanation.definitionFit: Kathleen Raine was a twentieth-century British writer of verse and a Blake scholar.

clue.text: Hotel bible has French writer's name on it

indicators.note: the bible has the following word attached, so removing it leaves the writer

parts.note: Gideon Bibles are left in hotel rooms
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel's bible has a French author's name inscribed on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gideons place Bibles in hotel rooms; take away the ON that the clue says is on it and André Gide is left.
explanation.definitionFit: André Gide was a Nobel-winning French novelist, author of The Immoralist.

clue.text: "Wreathe iron pokers into true love " (Coleridge)

parts.note: a line from Coleridge with its last word gone: the twisted sweetheart's tie of ribbon or rope

explanation.surface: A quotation from Coleridge with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The full phrase is 'true-love knots', the interlaced bow that lovers exchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie made by interlacing rope or ribbon; a true-love one is a decorative token.

clue.text: Location of Jefferies's shepherdess?

parts.note: Richard Jefferies wrote of rural life; a country girl might be hired or found at a market gathering

explanation.surface: Where a shepherd girl in Richard Jefferies's country writing might be found.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Jefferies was a Victorian writer on English country life.
explanation.definitionFit: A rural market and festival gathering, where farm workers were traditionally hired.

clue.text: Issued by Miss Lehmann, but only for one dance

definitions.text: Issued by Miss Lehmann, but only for one dance

parts.words: Issued by Miss Lehmann, but only for one dance
parts.note: Rosamond Lehmann's novel is called ___ to the Waltz

explanation.surface: A woman sends out a request to dance, but limits it to a single number.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosamond Lehmann's 1932 novel is Invitation to the Waltz.
explanation.definitionFit: A request to attend, which in Lehmann's title is extended to a single waltz.

clue.text: Size of book by French auteur

definitions.meaning: a traditional paper and book format
Jacques, director of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg

explanation.surface: The dimensions of a volume written by a French film director.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional paper size used for books, and the surname of Jacques, director of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg.

clue.text: Evaluation of Tess's men as terribly wrong

indicators.note: words that have gone terribly wrong are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the name Tess with its possessive s kept as a letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A judgement that Hardy's Tess's men were awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly wrong' rearranges TESSSMENAS; Tess of the d'Urbervilles suffers badly at the hands of Alec and Angel.
explanation.definitionFit: A judgement of worth or quality made after examination.
